section: Educational Psychology · Ch11 — Defense Mechanisms (Complete Set)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student who was badly bullied in Class 3 has no conscious memory of the incident at all years later, though it still subtly affects his behaviour. This unconscious blocking of a distressing memory from awareness is:
explanation: Repression is the unconscious exclusion of painful/threatening memories or impulses from conscious awareness — distinct from denial, which is a conscious-level refusal to accept a fact that IS still remembered.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch11 — Defense Mechanisms (Complete Set)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student who has clearly failed a major exam insists to friends, 'I definitely passed, there's no way I failed,' refusing to accept the obvious result. This is an example of:
explanation: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality that is plainly evident, protecting the person from immediate distress — unlike repression, which involves the memory being unconsciously blocked rather than consciously refused.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch11 — Defense Mechanisms (Complete Set)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A teacher who was scolded by the principal comes home and snaps angrily at her own children over a trivial matter, even though they did nothing wrong. Redirecting an emotion from its true source to a safer target is:
explanation: Displacement redirects an emotional response (anger at the principal) toward a substitute target (the children) that is safer to express it toward than the original source.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch11 — Defense Mechanisms (Complete Set)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student with strong aggressive impulses channels this energy into becoming a highly disciplined, competitive boxer instead of getting into fights. Redirecting an unacceptable impulse into a socially acceptable, even constructive, activity is:
explanation: Sublimation is considered the most 'mature' defense mechanism — it channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued, constructive outlet, unlike displacement, which simply redirects the emotion toward a different (but still potentially inappropriate) target.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch11 — Defense Mechanisms (Complete Set)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A child who secretly feels intense jealousy toward a new sibling instead behaves with exaggerated, almost excessive affection and care toward the baby. Expressing the opposite of one's true, unacceptable feeling is:
explanation: Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse (jealousy) into its opposite (exaggerated affection) at the conscious/behavioural level — the overly intense nature of the opposite behaviour is often a clue to the mechanism at work.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch11 — Defense Mechanisms (Complete Set)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A 6-year-old who has been toilet-trained for years starts bed-wetting again after the birth of a new sibling, reverting to an earlier developmental behaviour under stress. This is:
explanation: Regression is reverting to behaviour patterns characteristic of an earlier developmental stage when facing stress or anxiety — here, the arrival of a sibling triggers a return to earlier, more dependent behaviour.
